author: Sophia Buckley-Clement Staff Writer
title: Otter Valley School Board debriefs facilities tour | Local News | rutlandherald.com
text:
BRANDON — Members of the Otter Valley Unified Union School Board said Tuesday that a tour of district facilities revealed just how dire the condition of its high school is.
The June 20 tour was conducted as part of the board’s Task Force 2.0 initiative, which focuses on long-term facilities planning across the district with support from an external facilitator.
Members in attendance visited all OVU facilities during the tour.
“I would like to take some time to talk about each school we went to. What were your thoughts? There were some people who weren’t there, so they might be very curious,” said Board Chair Laurie Bertrand.
While members said each building had areas of improvement, Otter Valley Union High School was clearly in the worst condition.
In recent years, a major OVUHS renovation has been a topic of conversation for the board. Such a renovation would add new structures to the building to incorporate a middle school model.
“There are a bunch of systems that are inadequate and failing,” member Kevin Thornton said.
Among those items identified, Thornton noted the major leak in the cold water storage area, broken tiles in the girls’ locker room, holes in the Moosalamoo Room ceiling, and poorly maintained storage areas.
“In the furnace room, the pumps are from 1961,” Thornton said. “It’s no longer possible to get parts for those. They’re already using parts that don’t fit. … Both the head custodian and the facilities director said that the thing they worry about most is the electric.”
Bertrand said the tour revealed that the building is not well-maintained, adding that the district needs “to know how to live with it” at this point.
“(We) badly need an expert, thorough review of this building — way beyond what the state did. My suspicion is that this building might be past repairing,” Thornton said.
At Lothrop Elementary School, member Jessica Fjeld said that while there is a lot of empty classroom space, the school is using those rooms as regulatory spaces for students.
“We also got to go through the classroom that would have been the preschool if that had happened. We all noted the large space of it,” Bertrand said. “The bathroom was (also) adequate.”
Member Fernanda Canales said there is a need for new heating pumps for the fifth- and sixth-grade classrooms.
“Even though it’s the oldest building. I think it was best,” Thornton said.
Bertrand said the central office struggles with an excess of space, noting that the board has had previous conversations about moving it to OVUHS or Lothrop.
“It does feel disconnected from the students’ experience,” Fjeld said.
At Neshobe School, members noted that some of its air-handling systems are antiquated and take up significant space.
“We also talked a lot about the … (combination) gym lunchroom piece, and whether or not it works well for them,” Canales said.
Members also noted spatial constraints at Caverly School, a lack of library teaching space at Otter Creek Academy at Leicester, and the successes of Sudbury’s Bruce Academy program.
“(North Campus) is a building with problems. It is very old. It’s broken up into small rooms with brick walls, so it’s almost impossible to rearrange. The basement’s a mess,” Thornton said.
Members also said OCA Whiting is a great location for childcare, especially given the lack of such services in the area.
The OVU Board will next meet beginning at 5 p.m. on Aug. 25 for its annual board retreat.
